sentences: Do what you love and you will never work a single day.
This phrase is widely circulated.
However, it calls for caution, as it is more recent and more problematic than it seems.
For most of history, work was not meant to be fulfilling.
It served to meet basic needs.
The idea that a job should provide meaning and personal fulfillment appeared late, and especially in certain professional categories.
This evolution has its benefits: it has legitimized the refusal of degrading conditions.
But it also produces perverse effects.
The first is guilt.
If work is supposed to be a passion, not loving your job becomes a personal failure rather than an ordinary situation.
However, the majority of jobs, in any society, are necessary without being exciting.
The second effect is more concrete.
The sectors where passion is emphasized — culture, care, entertainment, research, sports — are often those where salaries are the lowest and conditions are the most difficult.
The supposed passion serves as an implicit argument there: since you love it, you will accept less.
Researchers have named this phenomenon and documented it in several countries.
Should we then give up on seeking meaning?
Certainly not.
But perhaps we need to shift the requirement.
A job can be bearable and well-paid, leaving time and energy for what matters elsewhere.
This is not a renunciation.
It's another way to refuse that work takes up all the space.

sentences: Remembering so that it doesn't happen again.
This phrase, often repeated in relation to the great tragedies of history, expresses a deep conviction: the memory of past horrors would protect us against their return.
It is in the name of this idea that we maintain the memory of the massacres, that we visit the sites of horror, that we pass on to younger generations the story of the worst.
But this conviction, however noble it may be, needs to be viewed with clarity.
Does memory really suffice to prevent the worst from happening again?
The idea is based on an appealing reasoning: if people know what certain ideas, certain hatreds, and certain cowardices have led to, they will be able to recognize and reject them.
Memory would thus be a vigilance, an immunity acquired at the cost of past misfortune.
And it is true that ignorance of the past encourages its repetition: a people that knows nothing of the disasters of history would be more exposed to retracing that path.
In this respect, memory is indeed a protection, and forgetting is a danger.
However, history itself warns us not to overestimate this power.
Because atrocities have been repeated even when the memory of previous ones was vivid.
Knowing the past has not always prevented us from starting again, and we have seen educated societies fall into horror once more.
Memory alone does not provide immunity.
It can even, if misdirected, foster new resentments, sustain old hatreds, and be used to justify new violence in the name of past wounds.
Memory is not always on the side of peace.
This is because memory can take very different forms.
Remembering as a victim, to harbor a grudge, does not have the same effect as remembering to understand.
A memory that merely rehashes emotion, without an effort to understand, offers little protection: it stirs emotions without enlightening.
What truly protects us is less the raw memory than what we make of it: understanding how the worst became possible, what mechanisms led to it, and what ordinary cowardices allowed it.
Remembering the facts is not enough; we must draw intelligence from them.
Memory is therefore only a protection under certain conditions.
It must be accompanied by understanding, aim to recognize the mechanisms of evil rather than just mourn the victims, and illuminate the present instead of trapping us in the past.
An intelligent memory looks less backward than forward: it examines the present to detect signs of what it knows.
To remember so as not to repeat: yes, but only if we truly remember, that is to say, if we understand.
Memory is not an automatic guarantee; it is a vigilance to maintain, a task that always needs to be resumed.
It only protects us if we make it work, not if we let it lie dormant in commemorations.

sentences: Medicine keeps pushing back the boundaries of death.
What was fatal yesterday can be treated today; life expectancy has dramatically increased, and some even dream of extending it indefinitely, or even abolishing death one day.
In light of these perspectives, a question that has long been theoretical arises with new urgency: should we want to live longer and longer?
Does the desire to push back death, as natural as it may be, have a limit that it would be wise to recognize?
The desire to live is the most fundamental there is, and it would be absurd to condemn it.
That medicine has so significantly delayed early death, spared so much suffering and grief, is an undeniable blessing.
No one seriously wishes to return to a time when people died young, when illness struck without recourse.
Wanting to live, and to live in good health for as long as possible, is legitimate, and the progress that makes this possible deserves to be praised.
The question is therefore not about giving up this desire, but about knowing whether it has a point beyond which it would turn against itself.
Extending life only makes sense if that extended life remains worth living.
Pushing back death at the cost of a diminished, dependent existence, devoid of what makes life valuable, is not necessarily progress.
Extending duration without extending quality can be a cruelty rather than a benefit.
That's why the real question may not be 'how long?', but 'what kind of life?'
— not the quantity of years, but what they contain.
Adding years to life is only worthwhile if we also add life to those years.
There is something even more dizzying: the idea of a life without end.
Some dream of abolishing death itself.
But would that really be desirable?
One can doubt it.
Many thinkers have argued that death, far from being just an evil, gives life a part of its meaning and flavor.
It is because our time is limited that each moment is valuable, that we make choices, that we commit ourselves.
An infinite existence, where nothing would ever be urgent, where everything could always be postponed, might lose what makes life precious: its irreplaceable and finite nature.
Death is not only what deprives us of life; it is also, paradoxically, what gives it its weight.
This does not mean we should stop postponing death, nor give up on the advancements that extend and improve life.
It means not to make mere duration an absolute, as if living longer were in itself the ultimate goal.
An ancient wisdom taught that one should seek less to add days to one's life than to give life to one's days.
This distinction remains valuable at a time when medicine gives us unprecedented powers over the duration of existence.
Should we want to live longer and longer?
Yes, as long as it means living fully, in good health, in a life that is worthwhile.
But perhaps not to the point of making duration everything, nor dreaming of an immortality that, by abolishing death, would also abolish what gives life its value.
Living well matters more than living long — and wisdom may consist in accepting that our time is limited, while still cherishing every moment it gives us.

sentences: Nothing is more familiar to us than time, and nothing is more difficult to think about.
"What is time, then?
If no one asks me, I know it; if I want to explain it to someone who asks me, I no longer know it."

This admission from an ancient thinker expresses the strange paradox of our relationship with time: we are immersed in it, we live it every moment, and yet, as soon as we try to grasp it, it slips away.
Let's explore this enigma starting from a dizzying observation: when we look closely, time seems to have no reality, each of its three dimensions dissolving under analysis.
Let's consider the past.
It was, but it is no longer; it has ceased to exist, and it only has the fragile being of memory.
What is past no longer exists anywhere, except in the trace it has left in us; the past, as such, does not have a present being.
Let's consider the future.
It will be, but it is not yet; it only has the uncertain being of expectation.
What is to come does not exist yet, it is only anticipated, imagined, foreseen; the future, as such, also does not have a present being.
Only the present remains, seeming to exist alone.
But what is the present?

A moment, one might say; but this moment, if we grasp it, reveals itself to be without thickness, a pure limit between a past that is no longer and a future that is not yet, an elusive point that vanishes as soon as we try to fix it.
The present, hardly is it, that it is already no more; it does not last, it passes, it flees.
Thus time, whose three dimensions dissolve — the past that is no longer, the future that is not yet, the present that vanishes — seems to have no reality, to be a pure flight without substance.
This vertigo is not just a trick of the mind; it touches on something real in our experience of time, which is indeed that of a flight, a flow that nothing stops.
We experience time as something that escapes us, something we cannot hold onto, that takes everything away — our days, our joys, our loved ones, ourselves.
Time is what passes, and its flight is the source of many of our anxieties: we would like to hold onto what flees, to stop the happy moment, to preserve what time takes from us, and we cannot.

The apparent unreality of time, this dissolution of its dimensions, philosophically expresses what we experience existentially: that time cannot be grasped, that it slips through our fingers, that it is pure flight.
And yet, time is not nothing; it is even, in a sense, the most real thing in our experience.
For if its dimensions dissolve when considered as things, time exists fully as lived experience, as the very fabric of our existence.

A thinker has suggested that time does not exist outside, as an objective thing, but in the soul, as a relation to what is no longer and what is not yet: the past exists as present memory, the future as present expectation, the present as attention.
Time would not be an external reality, but a dimension of consciousness, the way a mind holds onto the past, awaits the future, and stands in the present.
Thus, time, unreal as a thing, would be fully real as lived experience.
This concept shifts the vertigo without completely dissipating it, but it sheds light on our relationship with time.
If time is primarily experienced, then the way we experience it matters more than its objective nature.
We can inhabit time in various ways: fleeing the present by living in nostalgia for the past or anxiety for the future; or conversely, remaining in the present, the only place where we truly live.
For if the past is no longer and the future not yet, it is indeed in the present, however fleeting it may be, that our life unfolds; it is the only time we truly have.

All wisdom regarding time may lie here: not to abandon the present, the only real time, in favor of a bygone past or an uncertain future, but to fully inhabit the fleeting moment, since it is in it, and only in it, that we exist.
The present, it will be said, does not exist, since it vanishes as soon as we grasp it.

But perhaps the opposite should be concluded: that the present, however fleeting it may be, is the only place of reality, the only time where we truly live, and that wisdom consists not in retaining it — which is impossible — but in inhabiting it.
Time escapes us if we try to grasp it as a thing; it reveals itself to us if we consent to live it as a flow.

And living, at its core, may be nothing other than this: consenting to the flight of time while fully inhabiting each of its moments — accepting that we cannot hold onto the present, and loving it all the more as it passes.

sentences: I slipped between my sheets, very upset, very agitated, and very embarrassed, knowing well that I wouldn't sleep much, trying to figure out what mistake I might have made, when someone gently knocked on my door.
I asked, "Who is there?"
A light voice replied, "Me."
I hurriedly got dressed; I opened the door; she came in.
"I forgot," she said, "to ask you what you have in the morning: chocolate, tea, or coffee?"
I had impulsively embraced her, showering her with kisses, stammering, "I have... I have... I have..."
But she slipped from my arms, blew out my light, and disappeared.
I remained alone, furious, in the darkness, looking for matches, not finding any.
I finally found some and went out into the corridor, half mad, with my candlestick in hand.
What was I going to do?
I wasn't thinking anymore; I wanted to find her; I wanted her.
And I took a few steps without thinking about anything.
Then, I suddenly thought: "But what if I go into my uncle's? What would I say?..."
And I stood still, my mind blank, my heart racing.
After several seconds, the answer came to me: "Of course, I would say that I was looking for Rivet's room to talk to him about something urgent."

sentences: When the Malandains returned to their cottage, the last one in the hamlet of La Sablière, on the road to Fourville, the father, an old, thin, wrinkled peasant, sat down at the table while his wife took down the pot and his daughter Adélaïde got the glasses and plates from the sideboard, and he said, "This place at Master Omont's might be good, since he’s a widower, his daughter-in-law doesn’t like him, he’s alone, and he has means.
We might as well send Adélaïde there."
The woman placed the blackened pot on the table, removed the lid, and while steam from the soup, smelling of cabbage, rose to the ceiling, she thought.
The man continued, "He has means, for sure.
But one would need to be sharp, and Adélaïde isn’t at all."
The woman then articulated, "We could still consider it."
Then, turning to her daughter, a sturdy girl with a silly look, yellow hair, and cheeks as red as apple skin, she shouted, "Do you hear, you big oaf.
You’ll go to Master Omont’s to offer yourself as a servant, and you will do everything he commands you."
The girl started to laugh foolishly without answering.
Then the three of them began to eat.
After ten minutes, the father resumed, "Listen up, girl, and try not to mess up what I’m about to tell you..."
And he outlined to her in slow, careful terms a whole set of rules of conduct, anticipating every detail, preparing her for this conquest of an old widower who was not on good terms with his family.
The mother had stopped eating to listen, and she remained, fork in hand, her eyes on her man and her daughter in turn, following this instruction with focused and silent attention.
Adélaïde remained motionless, her gaze wandering and vague, docile and stupid.
As soon as the meal was over, the mother had her put on her bonnet, and they both set off to find Mr. Césaire Omont.
He lived in a kind of small brick pavilion attached to the farm buildings occupied by his farmers.
For he had retired from farming to live off his income.
He was about fifty-five years old; he was big, jovial, and gruff like a wealthy man.
He laughed and shouted as if to bring down the walls, drank cider and brandy in large glasses, and was still considered hot-blooded despite his age.
